docs.title: Digital Security Tool Directory
docs.text:
A maintained, plain-language directory of free and open-source (FOSS) digital security tools — organized around what you're actually trying to do, not around product names.

Most people don't know what kind of protection they need; they just know something feels wrong, or they have a task in mind and no idea which tool fits it. This directory works backward from that.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Guided Tool Finder — answer a few plain questions, get a prioritized recommendation with next steps, embedded directly on this site.
  • Comparison Table — compare every cataloged tool on encryption, audits, jurisdiction, cost, and self-hosting.
  • If You Don't Feel Safe — situation-first guidance, not just a tool list.

docs.title: A note on gaps
docs.text: Where no vetted FOSS tool exists for a real need (consumer anti-malware is the clearest example right now), that's stated explicitly rather than papered over with an unrelated recommendation. This directory is maintained on an ongoing basis — gaps get filled as the FOSS landscape changes, not treated as permanent.

docs.title: Browsing & Productivity
docs.text: Password and login-security tools for everyday use.

docs.title: KeePassXC
docs.text:
keepassxc.org

Encryption AES, local database Open source Yes Audited Yes Self-host N/A — local file Cost Free Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Full control of your password database, no cloud dependency. Avoid if: You want automatic multi-device sync without setting it up yourself.

docs.title: Bitwarden
docs.text:
bitwarden.com

Encryption End-to-end (zero-knowledge) Open source Yes Audited Yes, regular Self-host Yes Account needed Email Cost Freemium Platforms Android, iOS, Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: A password manager that syncs effortlessly across every device. Avoid if: You don't want any cloud-hosted copy, even encrypted — use KeePassXC instead.

docs.title: Aegis Authenticator
docs.text:
getaegis.app

Encryption Local, encrypted export Open source Yes Cost Free Platforms Android

Best for: Two-factor codes kept off any company's server. Avoid if: You're on iPhone — Aegis is Android-only.

docs.title: Circumvention & Anonymity
docs.text: Tools for reaching blocked content, hiding your identity online, or getting around network-level monitoring.

docs.title: Tor Browser
docs.text:
torproject.org

Encryption Multi-layer (onion) routing; not full end-to-end on the open web past the exit node Open source Yes Audited Yes, ongoing public audits Logging None (no account) Jurisdiction US nonprofit, decentralized network Cost Free Self-host N/A — joins existing network Account needed None Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux, Android

Best for: Reaching blocked sites and hiding your identity from the sites you visit — the strongest anonymity in this list. Avoid if: You need speed for calls/streaming, or Tor itself is blocked with no bridges available.

docs.title: Orbot
docs.text:
orbot.app

Encryption Routes chosen apps through Tor Open source Yes Audited Shares Tor Project audits Logging None Jurisdiction Guardian Project (US) Cost Free Self-host N/A Account needed None Platforms Android, iOS

Best for: Routing other apps — not just a browser — through Tor on a phone. Avoid if: You need full anonymous browsing — pair it with Tor Browser, don't use it alone.

docs.title: Psiphon
docs.text:
psiphon3.com

Encryption Obfuscated VPN/proxy tunnel Open source Yes Audited No independent public audit found Logging Aggregate/session metadata per policy Jurisdiction Canada Cost Free (ad-supported) / paid Self-host No Account needed None Platforms Windows, Mac, Android, iOS

Best for: Quickly unblocking sites when Tor is too slow or also blocked. Avoid if: You need strong anonymity — this is built for access, not for hiding who you are.

docs.title: Outline VPN
docs.text:
getoutline.org

Encryption Shadowsocks-based VPN tunnel Open source Yes Audited Client + server open, community reviewed Logging Depends who runs your server Jurisdiction Depends on server operator Cost Free self-hosted, or paid via a provider Self-host Yes Account needed None Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS

Best for: A newsroom or org self-hosting its own VPN server for a trusted group. Avoid if: You have no one to run a server — there's no public Outline network to join.

docs.title: Mullvad VPN
docs.text:
mullvad.net

Encryption WireGuard / OpenVPN tunnel Open source Yes (apps) Audited Yes, regular independent audits Logging No-logs, audited Jurisdiction Sweden Cost Paid, flat fee Self-host No Account needed Anonymous account number, no email Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS

Best for: Everyday privacy from your ISP and hiding your IP — the most transparent commercial VPN. Avoid if: You're in a country that actively blocks known VPN IPs, or need Tor-level anonymity.

docs.title: Communications & Messaging
docs.text: Tools for private messaging, calls, and email.

docs.title: Signal
docs.text:
signal.org

Encryption End-to-end Open source Yes Audited Yes, protocol widely audited Logging Minimal metadata, no message content Jurisdiction US nonprofit Cost Free Self-host No Account needed Phone number Platforms Android, iOS, Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Default choice for most people; easiest to get contacts onto. Avoid if: A phone number would identify or endanger you.

docs.title: SimpleX Chat
docs.text:
simplex.chat

Encryption End-to-end Open source Yes Audited Partial, ongoing Logging No persistent user ID Jurisdiction UK Cost Free Self-host Yes (relays) Account needed None Platforms Android, iOS, Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Talking to someone with zero identifying signup info. Avoid if: You need a large contact list already on a mainstream platform.

docs.title: Briar
docs.text:
briarproject.org

Encryption End-to-end Open source Yes Audited Partial Logging None Jurisdiction UK nonprofit Cost Free Self-host N/A — peer-to-peer Account needed None Platforms Android, Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: No or unreliable internet, or you expect connectivity to be cut. Avoid if: Contacts aren't tech-comfortable — pairing is more manual than Signal.

docs.title: Thunderbird + OpenPGP
docs.text:
thunderbird.net

Encryption End-to-end (message body) Open source Yes Audited Yes (OpenPGP widely reviewed) Logging N/A — your own email account Jurisdiction Depends on your email provider Cost Free Self-host Yes (your mail server) Account needed Existing email Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Encrypted email with people who already use PGP. Avoid if: Contacts won't set up PGP keys — subject lines/metadata stay unencrypted regardless.

docs.title: Data & File Management
docs.text: Tools for encrypting, backing up, sharing, and cleaning files.

docs.title: VeraCrypt
docs.text:
veracrypt.fr

Encryption AES, full-disk or container, at rest Open source Yes Audited Yes Jurisdiction N/A — local software Cost Free Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Hiding files on a laptop/USB drive that could be seized or lost. Avoid if: You need seamless cloud sync — encrypted volumes don't sync well.

docs.title: Cryptomator
docs.text:
cryptomator.org

Encryption AES, per-file, at rest Open source Yes Audited Yes Cost Free (freemium mobile) Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS

Best for: Encrypting files before they hit Dropbox/Drive/etc, including on mobile. Avoid if: You need whole-disk encryption, not per-file.

docs.title: OnionShare
docs.text:
onionshare.org

Encryption Tor-routed transfer Open source Yes Logging None Cost Free Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Sending a file or hosting a page to one person, with no third-party server involved. Avoid if: The recipient won't install Tor Browser to receive it.

docs.title: restic
docs.text:
restic.net

Encryption AES, client-side, at rest & in transit Open source Yes Self-host Yes Cost Free Platforms Windows, Mac, Linux

Best for: Automated encrypted backups you fully control. Avoid if: You want a point-and-click GUI — this is command-line only. (A simpler GUI backup option is a current gap in this directory.)

docs.title: If You Don't Feel Safe
docs.text: This page is organized by symptom, not by tool — start with what's actually happening. For the interactive, step-by-step version, use the Guided Tool Finder.

docs.title: "I'm getting login alerts, password resets, or 2FA codes I didn't request"
docs.text:
This is usually an account takeover, not a device problem.

  1. Change the password now, from a device you trust — not the one you suspect is compromised.
  2. Check the account's "active sessions" list and sign out anything unfamiliar.
  3. Turn on 2FA if it wasn't already (Aegis Authenticator, for Android).
  4. Check recovery email/phone and mail-forwarding rules for silent persistence.
  5. Repeat for any account this one can reset (usually your email).

→ Security in a Box: recovering from account compromise

docs.title: "Someone close to me always seems to know my location or activity"
docs.text:
Possible device monitoring by someone with access to you.

Warning

Checking for or removing spyware can alert whoever is monitoring you and escalate risk before you're safe. If there's any chance of physical danger, contact a domestic violence hotline or stalkerware-specialist service before acting alone — see Coalition Against Stalkerware.

  • If it's safe to check: look at installed apps, device admin permissions, and accessibility permissions for anything unfamiliar.
  • Longer-term, a fresh device and accounts your monitor has never had access to is safer than trying to "clean" one they've already compromised (GrapheneOS, for a hardened replacement Android).

→ Security in a Box: protect against physical threats

docs.title: "My device is acting strange — battery drain, heat, unknown apps, random restarts"
docs.text:
Possibly malware. This directory doesn't yet have a vetted FOSS anti-malware pick — that's a real gap, not an oversight.

  1. Review installed apps for anything unfamiliar, and check admin/accessibility permissions.
  2. Update the OS and all apps.
  3. Uninstall anything suspicious rather than investigating it.
  4. If symptoms continue, back up what matters (Cryptomator/restic) and factory reset.

→ Security in a Box: protect against malware

docs.title: "I was recently stopped, detained, or had a device searched"
docs.text:
Treat the device as compromised from the moment it was taken.

  1. Remote-lock or remote-wipe it now if you still can: findmydevice.google.com (Android) or icloud.com/find (iPhone) from another device. (Not open-source, but the fastest real option in the moment.) If the drive wasn't encrypted, assume its contents are already exposed.
  2. Change passwords for anything accessible from that device, from a different trusted device.
  3. Log out other sessions on major accounts.
  4. Assume contacts and message history were seen — consider a heads-up to anyone whose safety could be affected.
  5. For next time: Tails OS (amnesiac, boots from USB) or GrapheneOS (hardened daily-driver Android) limit what a future search can expose.

→ Security in a Box: what to do when you risk being arrested

docs.title: "I'm getting threats or messages with private details about me"
docs.text:
Mostly a process problem, not a tools problem.

  1. Document everything first — screenshots with timestamps and URLs visible, before reporting or blocking (reporting often removes the evidence).
  2. Lock down account privacy settings.
  3. Report and block through the platform's harassment-specific flow.
  4. Tighten account security as a precaution (Bitwarden/KeePassXC + Aegis) — doxxing often follows, or precedes, account compromise.

→ Security in a Box: protect yourself on social media

docs.title: No specific incident — general check-up
docs.text:
1. Unique passwords everywhere (KeePassXC or Bitwarden).
  2. 2FA on your important accounts, starting with email (Aegis Authenticator).
  3. Review connected apps and active sessions on your main accounts.
  4. Keep devices updated — most real-world compromises exploit already-patched holes.

→ Or walk the full Security in a Box check-up.
